Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is very effective and well-balanced. The primary interaction on the dock—which in "story time" only takes a couple of minutes—is slightly stretched using sensory details (the wet rope, the suitcase wheel getting stuck, the peeling paint on the house) and internal reflections. This stretching successfully creates a heavy, tense atmosphere that mirrors the emotional distance between mother and son, as well as the slow, indifferent movement of the river. 

At the same time, the author uses brief moments of time compression—such as summarizing the approach of the ferry in the third paragraph and condensing the time since the father's death into the image of the shutters he painted "last spring" now peeling—to seamlessly provide backstory without interrupting the quiet, deliberate pacing of the present scene.
